claim: Britain closed the Burma Road for three months in July 1940 under Japanese pressure and reopened it in October (18 October)
source: Wikipedia, Burma Road; cbi-theater.com 'Japan forces Britain to close Burma Road'; chinaww2.com daily chronology
note: No source found that names the day of the July agreement; the report says 'mid-July'. That the three months were the rainy season is from memory.

claim: Japan had already pressed France in June 1940 to stop the arms traffic through Indochina; Japanese bombing of the Burma Road is not confirmed
source: FRUS 1940 vol. IV (telegram from Tokyo, 20 June 1940); Wikipedia, Japanese invasion of French Indochina
note: The pressure on France is confirmed. A source for the bombing of the road and its bridges was not found; the third order and its flag are written as a modeled alternative.

claim: The Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact was signed in Moscow on 13 April 1941 for five years by Matsuoka and Molotov; Stalin saw Matsuoka off at the station
source: Wikipedia, Soviet-Japanese Neutrality Pact; Foreign Relations of the United States 1941 vol. IV

claim: In Berlin Ribbentrop pressed Matsuoka to take Singapore, and the Germans kept Barbarossa from the Japanese; Germany attacked the Soviet Union ten weeks after the pact; Soviet divisions moved from the Far East to the west in 1941 (14 to 30 divisions by different counts, and the reason is disputed)
source: IMTFE records via imtfe.law.virginia.edu; operationbarbarossa.net, 'The Siberian divisions and the battle for Moscow'; AFIO Intelligencer
note: The report says only that Moscow can move divisions west; it does not say the Sorge reports caused it.

claim: Nagumo's carriers raided Colombo on 5 April 1942 and Trincomalee on 9 April; the heavy cruisers Cornwall and Dorsetshire were sunk on 5 April and the carrier Hermes on 9 April; Somerville had hoped for a night action
source: Australian War Memorial; Royal Australian Navy Battle Summary No. 15 and 16; pacificeagles.net
note: The report says the raid took five carriers; one source gives six for the Japanese force. The Eastern Fleet's withdrawal to East Africa is from memory.

claim: The American Volunteer Group was recruited under a Chinese contract and trained at Toungoo in Burma; it first fought over Kunming on 20 December 1941 and was disbanded on 4 July 1942
source: Wikipedia, Flying Tigers; mysticstamp.com history note
note: That it flew over Rangoon until the city fell is from memory.

claim: A plan for American-manned bombers in China (JB 355) was approved by Roosevelt in July 1941 and not carried out before the war; Stimson and Marshall opposed it; T. V. Soong lobbied for it
source: Military History Now, 'Target: Japan'; Project MUSE, 'Preemptive Strike: the secret plan that would have prevented the attack on Pearl Harbor'
note: The approval date of 23 July comes from a forum post; the month is in the other sources. The report gives no plan number.

claim: Stilwell reached Chungking in early March 1942 as Chiang's chief of staff; Chiang placed the Chinese Fifth and Sixth Armies under his command in Burma; Stilwell was recalled in 1944
source: Wikipedia, China Burma India theater; HistoryNet, Stilwell's escape from Burma
note: The wording 'the first of a long series of quarrels' is a summary, not a source.

claim: USS Wasp, loaned to the British, flew off Spitfires toward Malta on 20 April 1942 (Operation Calendar) and made a second run in May (Operation Bowery); most of the first batch was destroyed on the ground within days
source: Wikipedia, Operation Calendar and Operation Bowery
note: Churchill asked Roosevelt for the carrier: from the same page. That Wasp reached the Pacific in the summer is from memory.

claim: The Pacific route carried about half of Lend-Lease aid to the Soviet Union by weight, exclusively in Soviet-flag ships after the United States entered the war
source: Wikipedia, Pacific Route; lend-lease.net route table (about 47 percent)
note: Japan inspecting some Soviet ships and leaving the route open is from memory and unchecked.

claim: The Arctic route carried about 23 percent and the Persian Corridor between 24 and 45 percent, depending on the source
source: Naval History and Heritage Command (Arctic); Wikipedia, Persian Corridor
note: The report states no Persian figure.
